title: Capacity orchestration emergency cookbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working cookbook for emergency capacity orchestration and infra-failure recovery focused on GPU/node replacement, safe cordon/drain, cluster-wide recovery patterns, and fast capacity add. Goal: give oncall engineers clear tactical steps to restore service while minimizing cascade impact.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated clusters running Redwood inference serving.
- Assumes k8s control plane healthy; if control plane is degraded, escalate to platform-eng immediately.
- Hardware replacement flows assume physical access via datacenter partners or cloud provider support.
- This doc is a practical checklist, not a design doc. Keep it short and testable.

Who owns what (roles):
- Oncall SRE (first responder): triage, apply immediate mitigations (cordon/drain, scaleouts), communicate incident.
- Capacity Lead (sre senior): approve emergency instance purchases or manual node pool edits.
- Infra Ops (hardware/vendor liaison): coordinate physical GPU swap or chassis replacement.
- Prod Eng / Serving runtime: validate model-serving fallbacks and health.

Quick triage matrix (first 10 minutes):
1) Are user-facing errors increased? Check alerts, P99 latency, error budget dashboards.
2) Is this localized to a zone/instance type or global? Check per-region dashboards.
3) Are pods failing with GPU attach or OOM errors? kubectl get events + node describe.
4) If a single node shows hardware failure signs (nvlink errors, GPU unreachable) -> consider cordon + drain.

Immediate mitigation checklist (fast actions):
- Set incident channel: #sre-incidents, create JIRA-OPS ticket.
- Fail closed or degrade gracefully: toggle route-policy to lower-cost/backfill region if necessary (console -> rollouts -> emergency-fallback).
- If GPU attach errors are causing pod churn, quickly cordon node: kubectl cordon <node-name>
- Drain safely with eviction timeout and pod disruption budgets: kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120
  - Note: if drains stall due to long-lived healthchecks, use --grace-period=30 temporarily and capture logs for postmortem.

GPU replacement (field hardware path) - fast checklist:
1) Validate node hardware state: ssh to node, dmesg | grep -i nvrm or check nvidia-smi exit codes. Capture logs to /tmp/node-failure-<time>.txt
2) If node is responsive but GPUs failing: mark as scheduling-disabled in k8s (kubectl label node <node> maintenance=true) to avoid new pods.
3) Inform infra-ops: vendor ticket + exact GPU serials; ask for expedited swap.
4) While waiting, shift load: drain node -> allow pods to restart on other nodes or autoscale.
5) Post-swap validation: run a small GPU smoke test job (serving-runtime/gpu-smoke-test image) that executes a generation request across models used by that node type.

Node cordon/drain detailed guidance (for ambiguous cases):
- Use kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> to list impacted pods.
- If pods have huge KV-cache or long startup: annotate pods with reroute=faststart to skip heavy cache restore for the emergency tenant. (This is a temporary runtime flag; coordinate with serving-runtime.)
- If PodDisruptionBudget blocks drain and business-critical tenants are affected, escalate to capacity lead; consider manual eviction of non-critical pods by deleting specific replicas from ReplicaSet with --cascade=orphan.

Cluster recovery and capacity add (software first):
1) Autoscaler check: confirm ClusterAutoscaler is healthy and not erroneously inhibited (kubectl -n kube-system get deployment cluster-autoscaler).
2) If autoscaler healthy but no nodes: check cloud provider limits (quotas). If quotas hit -> request quota bump via cloud console + inform capacity lead.
3) Manual nodepool scale: use infra provisioning docs -> edit nodepool template and increase desired count by increments of 2 for GPU pools to avoid long scheduling pauses.
4) Warmup new nodes by pre-pulling key container images and running the gpu-smoke-test before allowing scheduling. Script: infra/scripts/prewarm-node.sh <node-ip>

Emergency capacity by temporary instance types (stopgap):
- If preferred GPU SKU unavailable, consider heterogeneous fallback: spin up cheaper/older GPU SKUs and pin models to quantized variants for those nodes. Steps:
  1) Create node pool with label accelerator=fallback
  2) Add scheduling policy route: in console, create policy that routes low-priority workloads to nodeSelector accelerator=fallback.
  3) Deploy quantized model variant for those lanes so latency degrades but capacity preserved.
- Document performance delta and ticket the expected degradation to affected product owners.

Safety knobs and rollback triggers:
- Global traffic reroute engaged if P95 tail rises > 4x baseline for 10m.
- If node replacement causes >10% increased error rate in next 20m, revert routing and re-evaluate.
- Ensure circuit-breaker thresholds in front of model endpoints are active to prevent cascading retries.

Post-incident validation checklist (what to verify before closing):
- All nodes back to Ready with expected labels and taints.
- KV-cache hit rate recovered to pre-incident baseline.
- No latent pod OOMs or CrashLoopBackOffs for 60m after repair.
- Cost impact estimate and capacity runbook updated with any new manual steps performed.
- Create a short incident blameless postmortem draft (include root-cause hypothesis, timeline, mitigations, follow-ups).

Runbook testing and maintenance notes:
- This cookbook must be exercised in the next SRE game-day. Create ticket JIRA-OPS-2019 to schedule.
- During tests, validate that the prewarm script reduces cold-start p99 by at least 40% for the targeted model family.
- Ownership: oncall -> update this doc if any ad-hoc commands were executed. Add example commands to the infra repo.

Common gotchas and troubleshooting pointers (rapid references):
- k8s cordon looks OK but pods still stuck -> check PodGC issues or finalizers preventing termination. kubectl get pod <pod> -o json | jq .metadata.finalizers
- GPUs present but nvidia-smi hangs -> kill long-running container that may be blocking the device-mapper and reboot the node if necessary (last resort).
- ClusterAutoscaler not adding nodes -> check taints/tolerations mismatch or ResourceQuota at namespace level.

Open questions / TODOs (for follow-up):
- Should we formalize a quantized-variant catalog and automated rollout for heterogeneous fallback? (owners: serving-runtime, product-optimize)
- Add a k8s operator to prewarm NV cache on node add? Prototype ticket created but not prioritized.
- Check provider support SLAs for physical GPU replacements in each region and add to runbook contacts.

Appendix: quick commands cheat-sheet
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120
- kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -i "gpu|nvidia|taint|condition"
- ssh <node> sudo journalctl -u kubelet -S "1 hour ago" | tail -n 200
- infra/scripts/prewarm-node.sh <node-ip>

Notes to self (informal):
- We keep relying on manual scaling in rush hours — long-term automation (predictive scaling from model load forecasts) is a must.
- When you drain critical nodes, expect bursty scheduling; watch image-pull rate limits — consider a private registry cache.

References and links (living):
- Serving runtime playbook (internal): confluence://serving-runtime/fallbacks (placeholder)
- Incident ticket template: JIRA-OPS-TEMPLATE
- Slack runbook channel: #sre-runbooks

End of draft.

(If you used or tested any command from here, paste output into JIRA-OPS ticket before closing.)
